opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's important to be honest about where we are.

The big advantage of the diffusion approach is speed. Because we're generating many tokens in parallel and refining them over a number of steps, instead of producing one token at a time, we get a very different latency and throughput profile than autoregressive models. That's what makes Mercury attractive for things like coding assistants, agentic loops, and voice, where latency really matters.

But there are real limitations. The first is that the frontier of raw capability is still set by the very largest autoregressive models. Those have had years of investment in scaling, data pipelines, post-training recipes, and RL. The whole ecosystem was built around next-token prediction. So on the hardest reasoning benchmarks, we're not at the absolute top of the leaderboard. We're competitive with models in a similar speed or cost class, and much faster, but there's a gap at the very high end.

The second is that a lot of the tooling and know-how doesn't transfer directly. Things like KV caching, speculative decoding, and many fine-tuning and alignment techniques were designed with left-to-right generation in mind. We've had to rethink a lot of that for diffusion: how you do reinforcement learning, how you handle very long contexts efficiently, and how you trade off the number of denoising steps against quality. There's still a lot of room to improve there, and it's something we're actively working on.

Third, there's a quality-versus-steps trade-off that's inherent to diffusion. If you push for maximum speed with very few refinement steps, you can see some degradation, especially on long, highly structured outputs where everything has to be globally consistent. Of course, that's also where diffusion can shine, because the model can go back and fix earlier parts of the sequence, which an autoregressive model can't do. But getting that balance right is still an engineering and research challenge.

So my view is that these are mostly limitations of maturity rather than fundamental ceilings. The diffusion paradigm is a few years behind in terms of total investment. Every time we scale up and bring over better training and post-training techniques, the gap closes. I'm quite optimistic that diffusion will be competitive on quality while keeping a big advantage on speed and cost. But today, if you need the absolute strongest reasoning model regardless of latency, the large autoregressive models are still the reference point.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being honest about where things stand, because diffusion language models are still a pretty young paradigm compared to autoregressive models, which have had, you know, close to a decade of concentrated engineering behind them.

The first thing I'd say is scale. Mercury 2 is very good at the frontier of speed. We get thousands of tokens per second on standard hardware because we're generating many tokens in parallel rather than one at a time. But on raw capability, on the hardest reasoning benchmarks, the biggest autoregressive frontier models are still ahead. Part of that is simply that we haven't trained at the same compute scale yet. We're a smaller team, and the question of whether diffusion scaling laws track or exceed autoregressive scaling laws at the very largest sizes is still, I'd say, an open empirical question. We have strong evidence that they're competitive, but nobody has run the experiment at the trillion-parameter level.

The second thing is the infrastructure ecosystem. Everything in the serving stack, from KV caching to speculative decoding to the way people do RLHF, was built around left-to-right generation. We had to rebuild a lot of that ourselves. So when someone compares us to an autoregressive model running on vLLM or something, they're comparing against years of community optimization. We're closing that gap, but it's real.

Third, there's a subtler point around the sampling procedure. In a diffusion model you choose how many denoising steps to take, and that's a dial between quality and latency. We've gotten pretty good at making few steps work, but there are tasks, particularly very long-horizon reasoning with lots of dependencies between tokens, where the parallel decoding can make locally plausible but globally inconsistent choices if you push the step count too low. Autoregressive models get a kind of free coherence from conditioning on everything before. We have to earn that through the denoising schedule and the training objective.

And then there's the long context story. Our context windows are reasonable, but the attention patterns in a bidirectional diffusion setup have different memory characteristics than causal attention, so extending to very long contexts is an area where we're actively working and I wouldn't claim we're at parity.

What I'd push back on is the idea that these are fundamental limitations. I think most of them are maturity limitations. The thing I find exciting is that the parallel generation gives you capabilities that are genuinely hard for autoregressive models, like editing in the middle of a sequence, or doing infilling natively, or having the model revise its own draft. So I'd say we're in a position where the speed advantage is already decisive for a lot of applications, especially agentic and code workflows where latency compounds, and the capability gap is something I expect to close as we scale and as the tooling matures.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the limitations of the diffusion approach from the broader limitations of language models. Generating text through iterative refinement gives us a different way to think about speed and quality, but it doesn’t automatically solve factual accuracy, reasoning, or reliability. A model can still produce a fluent answer that’s wrong.

There’s also a tradeoff in how much refinement you allow. The important question is whether you can get the quality you need within your latency and compute budget—and that depends on the task. Producing a plausible paragraph is different from writing code where one incorrect detail breaks the result.

So I’d be cautious about treating speed as a complete measure of progress. You also need to understand where the model fails, how consistently it follows constraints, and when its outputs need verification. I wouldn’t give a precise Mercury 2–specific assessment without grounding it in evaluations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate the limitations of the generation process from the limitations of the model itself. Diffusion gives us a different way to generate text, with opportunities to do more work in parallel and revise a candidate answer. But that doesn’t automatically solve hallucination, factual grounding, or difficult reasoning. Those still depend on what the model has learned and how we train and evaluate it.

There’s also a speed–quality tradeoff. How much computation do you spend refining an answer, and how do you decide when it’s good enough? Generating tokens in parallel creates an opportunity for efficiency, but you still have to maintain consistency across the response.

So I wouldn’t interpret faster generation as a claim that all the other limitations of language models have disappeared. We need to evaluate those capabilities separately, and be clear about where the model is reliable and where it still needs verification.
